## Guidelines for Module Organization and Improving Badly Structured Software

### Part 1 — Organizing Modules for Maintainability

---

**1. Keep modules small and name them clearly.**
Smaller components are easier to understand and, as a direct consequence, easier to maintain. Each component must be named and must expose [SWEBOK excerpt 9964a6f7f84d259b3754].

**2. Give every module a single, clearly bounded responsibility.**
Following Parnas's principle, each module in a system should carry one responsibility. Modularization is a special case of *separation of concerns* and *divide and conquer*: distinct functionalities and responsibilities belong in distinct components.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 39742602fae3ff95f6c7]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Component Modularization and Single Responsibility Principle.md`)

Encapsulation (or information hiding) builds upon [SWEBOK excerpt 31aba1aebbd0641d8e59]. Separating interface from implementation means that clients know and use the public interface without depending on how the component is built internally.

**6. Work at clearly defined levels of abstraction, using standard interfaces between levels.**
When working with one level of abstraction, details of levels above and below are encapsulated. Standard interfaces (e.g., APIs) between abstraction levels offer portability, easier integration, and wider reuse. ### Part 2 — Improving a Badly Structured Program Without Users Noticing

---

**9. Use refactoring — reorganize the program's internals without changing its behavior.**
Refactoring is a re-engineering [SWEBOK excerpt 692ff7ac0d06d7434633]. It [SWEBOK excerpt d4e5cc4de2badb331c65] can be used during maintenance activities specifically to reduce technical debt before and after code changes.

### Summary

| Concern | Key principle |
|---|---|
| Module size | Small, named, well-interfaced |
| Responsibility | One per module (Parnas) |
| Inter-module dependency | Minimize coupling |
| Intra-module consistency | Maximize cohesion |
| Internal details | Hide behind interfaces (information hiding) |
| Complexity management | Abstraction levels + standard interfaces |
| Cross-cutting issues | Separation of concerns |
| Design consistency | Uniformity / SOLID patterns |
| Invisible restructuring | Refactoring (behavior-preserving) |
| Ongoing health | Continuous refactoring to reduce technical debt |
| Safe restructuring | Reverse-engineer first to understand, then restructure |
